Dear Dr Tanaka,

Thank you for handling our submission, and our thanks to both referees for careful and constructive reports. Between them they covered the methods, the code and the text, and several of their comments led us to problems we wouldn't have found on our own. We took every point seriously, checking each one against the package and the manuscript, rerunning the measurements where a comment depended on them, and revising the package, its documentation and the article to address them.

This document reproduces every comment in full, followed by our response. We've numbered the comments so the responses can refer to each other (R1.1 to R1.13 for Referee 1, and R2.1 to R2.12 and R2.C1 to R2.C10 for Referee 2), and section numbers refer to the revised manuscript. Where we decided not to follow a suggestion, the response explains why. The changes to the package are in the development version on GitHub (<https://github.com/pedreirajr/cnefetools>) and will be released on CRAN as version 0.3.0.

# Referee 1

## General

> Evaluating the manuscript and accompanying software against [The R Journal guidelines](https://journal.r-project.org/R_package_guidelines.html), `cnefetools` demonstrates strong adherence. The paper balances geospatial context with a clear focus on the software's design, dual DuckDB/R backend, and performance benchmarks. The package addresses the data engineering challenge of processing 110 million Brazilian address records, making it a critical resource for researchers focused on Brazilian geospatial analysis. Beyond its immediate utility, `cnefetools` serves as a technical blueprint for the R developer community, demonstrating a performant architecture for the emerging class of DuckDB-powered data access packages. I have independently verified the examples in `read_cnefe()` and the primary vignettes; the package is fully functional and the API is intuitive. Furthermore, the codebase follows modern R development standards, including semantic messaging via `cli` and comprehensive `roxygen2` documentation.

**Response:** Thank you. We're glad the referee ran the examples and the articles independently, and we've tried to keep the package to that standard throughout this revision.

## Methodological considerations: land use mix indices

### R1.1: Binary classification and loss of granularity

> The core analytical module of the package, `compute_lumi()`, is built around a binary classification: Residential (Type 1) versus Non-Residential (Types 2–8). While the manuscript (Section 4) and the referenced preprint (Pedreira Junior et al. 2025) are transparent about this choice, the implementation results in a significant loss of the "fine-grained" information that the authors initially promote as a key advantage of the CNEFE dataset. Collapsing eight distinct categories—ranging from schools and hospitals to religious temples and factories—into a single "Non-Residential" bin means that diversity indices like **Entropy** and **HHI** do not actually measure functional land-use diversity, but rather simple "residential dominance." As a result, a neighborhood with ten different types of services would receive a lower "mix" score than one with a single service and a few houses, which is counter-intuitive for urban planning research and deviates from the multi-category standards discussed in the cited literature (e.g., Song et al. 2013).

**Response:** **We keep the binary formulation, and we agree with the referee's description of what it measures.**

The referee is right that with two categories the Entropy Index and the HHI measure how evenly an area is split between housing and everything else, not how diverse its non-residential uses are. That is the construct the indices are meant to capture, and it's the one on which they were defined and validated against job accessibility in Pedreira Junior et al. (2026), now published in *Land Use Policy*. Redefining the indices inside a software paper would change the object the paper describes, so we haven't done that.

What we have changed is how clearly this is stated, since a reader shouldn't have to infer it. Section 4.3 now says that the indices rest on a binary split, that they measure the balance between housing and all other uses rather than the diversity of those uses, and that an area whose non-residential addresses are all of one type scores the same as one where they are spread across every type, provided both have the same residential share. It also acknowledges that this differs from the multi-category definitions common in urban research, citing Song et al. (2013), and points users who need that diversity to the per-type counts that `cnefe_counts()` returns. Section 6 discusses where the binary split falls short, with the examples Referee 2 gives in R2.1, and multi-category formulations stay on the list of future work.

### R1.2: Reliance on Unreviewed Methodology

> **Reliance on Unreviewed Methodology:** The package serves as a "pixel-perfect" implementation of the authors' own directional indices (aHHI and BGBI), which are currently documented in an unreviewed engrXiv preprint (Pedreira Junior et al. 2025). While this demonstrates high internal consistency between the paper and the code, it also positions the package as a highly specialized tool for one specific methodological framework rather than a general-purpose geospatial utility. Given that these indices (specifically the BGBI) rely on a nonlinear transformation centered on a global proportion, their scientific validity rests entirely on the unreviewed preprint's claims. For a research-focused package, this narrow methodological scope should be more explicitly signaled to the user.

**Response:** **We've separated the two indices, because the referee's premise now holds for one of them and not the other.**

The BGBI has since been peer-reviewed and published (Pedreira Junior et al., 2026, *Land Use Policy* 169, 108135), where it is computed alongside four established indices and validated against job accessibility measures. The manuscript now cites that article for it.

The adapted HHI is still documented only in the engrXiv preprint (Pedreira Junior et al., 2025), which the manuscript keeps and now labels as a preprint. Nevertheless, it consists of a trivial monotone rescaling of the standard HHI, which runs from 0.5 to 1 with two categories, into the range 0 to 1, with a sign that shows which use dominates. It inherits the properties of an established index and adds only a direction, so it doesn't carry a validity claim of its own.

On scope, three of the six indices (entropy, HHI and the Balance Index) are standard measures from the literature, and the Index of Concentration at Extremes comes from Massey (2001), so only the BGBI and the adapted HHI are ours. The methodological basis of the indices is now explicit in Section 4.3 and in `?compute_lumi`, as described under R1.3.

### R1.3: Ambiguity in Documentation

> **Ambiguity in Documentation:** The user-facing documentation (`?compute_lumi`) fails to mention the binary simplification. A user reading the package's description of the 8 CNEFE categories would naturally assume the "Entropy Index" utilizes all available data. This creates a significant risk of misinterpretation: a researcher might publish results claiming "high land-use diversity" in a zone that is actually functionally homogeneous but balanced between residential and one other use. I recommend that the authors:
>
> 1. Update the function documentation to explicitly warn about the binary split.
> 2. Provide a theoretical justification for why the binary split was chosen over a multi-category approach, especially given that the raw CNEFE data already provides the necessary granularity. This is covered in the preprint, but a brief summary in the package documentation and the package paper would help users understand the rationale without needing to read the full paper.
> 3. Acknowledge that while this logic is consistent with their preprint, it may not align with the prevalent multi-category definitions of Land Use Mix in broader urban science.

**Response:** **Accepted, all three points.**

`?compute_lumi` now carries a `@details` section, which it previously lacked entirely. On the referee's point 1, it states the rule without ambiguity: an address is counted as residential when `COD_ESPECIE == 1` and as non-residential otherwise. On point 2, the justification now cites the peer-reviewed article rather than the preprint, since the indices are defined and empirically validated on that two-category basis in Pedreira Junior et al. (2026), *Land Use Policy* 169, 108135. The same `@details` block also documents the type 7 exclusion raised in R2.2 and the citywide baseline P raised in R2.3, so the help page and the article now state one contract instead of two.

We note that auditing the exclusion path in order to document it accurately uncovered a genuine defect, reported under R2.2 below.

The manuscript carries the same three points in Section 4.3: the rule, the justification with its citation, and the acknowledgement that the formulation differs from the multi-category definitions common in urban research (Song et al., 2013). It also tells users who need the diversity of non-residential uses that `cnefe_counts()` returns counts for all eight address types.

## Methodological considerations: H3 grids

### R1.4: H3 is not equal-area, and equal-area alternatives deserve a mention

> While providing H3 hexagonal aggregation is a practical and powerful feature, the H3 system (originally developed by Uber for logistical purposes) has notable limitations for rigorous spatial analysis. Because it uses a polyhedral gnomonic projection, it is not an equal-area grid. Cell areas can vary significantly, with distortions reported up to 50% across the globe. This is particularly relevant for a country with the vast latitudinal extent of Brazil. As Kmoch et al. (2025) emphasises, these distortions can introduce analytical biases in density modelling or aggregations where area uniformity is assumed.
>
> The authors demonstrate an excellent level of methodological rigour when discussing interpolation methods (Introduction and Section 4). They clearly articulate why dasymetric interpolation using CNEFE dwelling points as ancillary data is superior to simpler areal-weighted approaches. The internal implementation of these spatial operations is also robust, automatically reprojecting user-supplied polygons to a consistent CRS (EPSG:4326) to prevent silent join failures. I believe the discussion would benefit from a similar level of rigour regarding the choice of H3 as the default grid system.
>
> By including H3 as a primary built-in option, `cnefetools` understandably provides a practical solution for many users. However, it is also helpful to keep in mind that spreading awareness of H3's spatial drawbacks can prevent unintentional analytical biases. While it is entirely up to the authors' discretion whether to expand on this in the manuscript or documentation, I believe that briefly mentioning equal-area alternatives could be a valuable service to the community. Equal-area alternatives such as **ISEA**, the **A5** grid (available via the [a5R](https://belian-earth.github.io/a5R/) package), or the newer **IGEO7** system (Kmoch et al. 2025) help users make more informed decisions when high-precision area consistency is required.

**Response:** **Accepted. We add the caveat and the pointers.**

The referee is right, and we thank them for framing it as a service to users rather than as a defect. H3 uses a gnomonic projection onto an icosahedron, so cell areas are not constant, and across a country the size of Brazil that's worth stating rather than assuming.

Section 4.2, right where the manuscript quotes the average cell area, now carries a short paragraph noting that H3 is not equal-area, that this matters whenever an analysis assumes cells of equal size, as in density estimates, and pointing readers to equal-area alternatives when that is a requirement, namely the A5 grid through the a5R package (Graham, 2026), now on CRAN and cited and IGEO7, which is built on the ISEA projection (Kmoch et al., 2025).

Rather than quote a global figure, we measured the variation where it matters for our users. Across Brazil, resolution 9 cells range from about 80,000 m² to 127,000 m², so the largest is about 1.6 times the smallest, and 1.47 times between the 1st and 99th percentiles. The manuscript reports that range. It comes from the areas, computed with `h3jsr::cell_area()`, of the 19,998 distinct cells hit by a random sample of 20,000 points inside the national boundary.

We keep H3 as the built-in option, and the manuscript now says why. The DuckDB `h3` extension assigns cells inside the query, which keeps the aggregation in-process, and H3 cell identifiers can be joined with other data indexed on the same grid.

## Minor comments

### R1.5: Inconsistent software citation

> The authors are inconsistent in citing software used or discussed in the manuscript. While they cite `sf`, `areal`, `geobr`, `populR`, `duckdb`, and `h3jsr`, implementation-relevant packages such as `arrow`, `duckspatial`, and `piggyback` are mentioned without formal citations. The model-based change-of-support package `smile` is also discussed in the related-work section without a citation. These omissions should be corrected to ensure proper attribution of open-source software.

**Response:** **Accepted without reservation. This was an oversight on our part.**

All four packages are on CRAN and therefore have canonical citations. `arrow`, `duckspatial`, `piggyback` and `smile` now have bibliography entries taken from each package's own citation, and each is cited at its first mention in the text. We also added citations for `censobr`, which the new provenance statement relies on (R1.9), and for `a5R` (R1.4).

R2.11 raises the `smile` citation independently and is answered by the same change.

## Code: usability

### R1.6: Workflow & API: `polygon_type` is redundant

> **Workflow & API:** The package has a highly intuitive and user-friendly workflow. The dual-backend architecture is abstracted cleanly behind a single `backend = "duckdb"` or `"r"` argument. However, the `polygon_type` argument feels somewhat redundant. If a user passes an `sf` object to the `polygon` argument, it naturally implies they want to use custom polygons rather than an H3 grid. While the package currently infers this and issues a warning, the authors could consider making this inference automatic and silent. Alternatively, they could deprecate `polygon_type` entirely in favour of simply checking whether `polygon` is `NULL` or an `sf` object.

**Response:** **Accepted, and we took the stronger of the two options the referee offers.**

The referee is right that `polygon_type` is redundant: passing an `sf` object to `polygon` already states the intent. Rather than only silencing the existing inference, we deprecated the argument.

The mode is now inferred from whether `polygon` is `NULL`. Code that still passes `polygon_type` keeps working and emits a `lifecycle` deprecation warning, so nothing breaks for existing users. The three alert lines the function used to print when it inferred the mode are gone, since there is no longer an inconsistency to announce.

Two behaviours are preserved deliberately. `polygon_type = "user"` with no `polygon` remains an error, because it states an intent the call cannot satisfy and it errored before. `polygon_type = "hex"` alongside a supplied `polygon` resolves to user polygons, which is what the previous inference did.

### R1.7: Cache Location Override

> **Cache Location Override:** The package downloads potentially massive ZIP files (up to 901 MB uncompressed) and hardcodes the cache location to `tools::R_user_dir("cnefetools", "cache")`. While caching is a very useful feature and using this directory aligns with CRAN policies for persistent data, forcing users to store large files on their primary partition can be problematic for those with limited space. The authors might consider allowing users to override this cache path. While packages dealing with large geospatial datasets like `osmextract` rely on environment variables to set the download directory, providing an explicit user-facing function argument (e.g., `cache_dir`) might be more intuitive for novice R users. This ensures they can easily point the download to a larger secondary drive or shared volume.

**Response:** **Accepted. Both mechanisms the referee mentions are now available.**

The cache location resolves from the most specific source to the least:

1. a `cache_dir` argument on the calling function,
2. the `CNEFETOOLS_CACHE_DIR` environment variable,
3. `tools::R_user_dir("cnefetools", which = "cache")`, the previous default.

We implemented both on purpose. The referee cites `osmextract`, which uses an environment variable, and also observes that an explicit argument is more discoverable for less experienced users. The argument outranks the variable so a single call can be redirected without changing the session. `cache_dir` reaches `read_cnefe()`, `cnefe_counts()`, `compute_lumi()`, `tracts_to_h3()`, `tracts_to_polygon()`, and also `clear_cache_muni()` and `clear_cache_tracts()`. 

The CRAN-policy default is unchanged, so users who do nothing see exactly the previous behaviour. Section 3 of the manuscript describes the order and why both mechanisms exist, and a new article on the package website, "Cache and exported copies", shows how to use them.

### User feedback and documentation (no action requested)

> **User Feedback:** The extensive use of the `cli` package for informative progress steps, success messages, and structured aborts provides an excellent developer experience.
>
> **Documentation:** The functions are thoroughly documented with roxygen2, clearly explaining parameters, return types, and caching behaviour.

**Response:** Thank you. The functions and arguments added in this revision follow the same conventions and are documented in the same way.

## Code: technical implementation

### Organisation and style (no action requested)

> **Organisation & Style:** The code is meticulously organised and adheres strongly to modern Tidyverse conventions. Internal helpers are properly prefixed with `.` and annotated with `@noRd` to keep the exported namespace clean. The use of `rlang::check_installed()` for managing optional dependencies (e.g., `sf`, `duckdb`, `piggyback`) is excellent.

**Response:** Thank you.

### R1.8: Resilience to URL Changes and Data Versioning

> **Resilience to URL Changes and Data Versioning:** The package relies entirely on a pre-built internal index (`cnefe_index_2022`) to resolve IBGE FTP download URLs. If IBGE changes their directory structure or filenames, existing versions of the package will fail to download data. Currently, the package handles failures gracefully via `httr2`. It attempts hardcoded retries (300s, 600s, 1800s) before aborting, but lacks a dynamic fallback mechanism. Furthermore, while the manuscript states that `cnefetools` "targets the 2022 edition and future censuses," the current architecture is strictly hardcoded for 2022. The internal `.get_cnefe_index()` and `.validate_year()` functions explicitly abort for any year other than 2022. If the 2030 census introduces a different schema or FTP hierarchy, the package will require a significant update. The authors might consider adding a dynamic fallback that scans the FTP server at runtime to reconstruct URLs or at least acknowledging that support for "future censuses" is currently a roadmap item rather than a present capability. Additionally, adding a pre-flight availability check could vastly improve the user experience. If the base IBGE server is unreachable, inform the user they may have a connectivity issue. If the server is reachable but the specific file is not (e.g., a 404 error), inform the user that the upstream directory structure may have changed and encourage them to report the issue on the package's issue tracker. I have included a small supplementary script (`test_url_fallback.R`) that illustrates the current behaviour when an internal IBGE URL is broken. It should not be treated as a production test in its current form because it mutates internal package data and can trigger the long retry timeouts, but it may be useful as a starting point for a mocked `testthat` regression test with shorter retry intervals.

**Response:** This comment makes three requests of very different cost, so we answer them separately below, as R1.8a, R1.8b and R1.8c.

### R1.8a: Dynamic FTP fallback

**Response:** **We haven't added a runtime scan of the FTP server, and we've handled the underlying risk in two other ways.**

A dynamic fallback would have to rebuild URLs from a directory layout that has, by assumption, just changed in some unknown way, so it could only guess, and a wrong guess is harder for a user to diagnose than a clear failure. We think the referee's concern is better met by what we did under R1.8c and R1.11. The pre-flight check now tells the user when a file is missing because the layout changed upstream and asks them to report it, so the index can be rebuilt with `data-raw/cnefe_index_2022.R` and shipped in a patch release. Until then, `read_cnefe(file = ...)` reads a ZIP the user downloads by hand, exactly as IBGE publishes it, without going through the index at all. Section 3 of the manuscript now describes both.

### R1.8b: "Future censuses" claim versus hardcoded 2022

**Response:** **Accepted, and answered with code rather than with wording.**

The referee is right that the claim sat uneasily beside a hardcoded year. Rather than soften the sentence, we removed the hardcoding. `.read_muni_boundary_2024()`, which called geobr with `year = 2024L` fixed, is now `.read_muni_boundary(code_muni, year)`, and `build_h3_grid()` gained a `year` argument that `cnefe_counts()`, `compute_lumi()` and `tracts_to_h3()` thread down from their own validated `year`.

This also corrects a mismatch the referee did not raise. The grid was previously built from a 2024 territorial base while the data aggregated onto it, and in `tracts_to_h3()` the census tracts interpolated onto it, belong to 2022. IBGE geocoded the CNEFE records against the base of their own year, so the grid now shares the reference frame of the data.

The change is behaviour-affecting in principle. Measured at resolution 9, the 2022 and 2024 grids are identical for both municipalities used in the package articles, Lauro de Freitas-BA at 550 cells and Fortaleza-CE at 2651 cells, so no published figure moves.

### R1.8c: Pre-flight availability check

**Response:** **Accepted, and the practical gain is larger than the message wording.**

We probed the live IBGE server before designing this, and it answers `HEAD` correctly: 200 with a content-length for a file that exists, 404 for one that does not, and a transport-level failure when the host cannot be resolved. The three cases the referee describes are therefore genuinely distinguishable at low cost.

- **Server unreachable.** The message names the host and points at connectivity, proxies and firewalls.
- **404.** The internal index is built from the published directory layout, so a 404 on a URL the package generated means that layout changed upstream. The message states that this is a problem with `cnefetools` rather than with the user's setup, and asks them to report it with the URL. Each case also carries a distinct condition class, so downstream code can branch on it.

The check runs **before** the retry ladder. Previously a URL that could never resolve consumed timeouts of 300, then 600, then 1800 seconds before failing. It now fails in seconds.

On the supplementary script, we followed the referee's own caution and did not adapt `test_url_fallback.R` directly, since it mutates internal package data and can trigger those long timeouts. The regression test mocks `httr2::req_perform()` instead, so it touches no network and enters no retry. One of its assertions counts requests, proving that a failed pre-flight is followed by zero download attempts.

We are grateful for the script regardless: it made the failure modes concrete and saved us from having to reproduce them.

### R1.9: External Data Provenance and Reproducibility

> **External Data Provenance and Reproducibility:** In addition to the municipal CNEFE ZIP files downloaded from IBGE, the package relies on derived internal data objects and GitHub-release assets, including the pre-built `cnefe_index_2022` and the UF-level census-tract Parquet files used by `tracts_to_h3()` and `tracts_to_polygon()`. The manuscript describes these assets functionally, but it does not yet give readers enough information to reproduce or audit their generation. I recommend adding a short data provenance statement that identifies the source files, generation scripts, package/data versions, release tags, and checksums or hashes for externally downloaded and derived assets. This is especially important because the package is positioned as infrastructure for reproducible spatial analysis. The authors may find the `geobr` project useful as a model: it uses a reproducible `targets` workflow and supporting infrastructure to generate and maintain its data assets. Adopting a similar approach, or at least documenting the existing asset-generation pipeline more explicitly, would make `cnefetools` more robust to upstream data changes and easier for future contributors to maintain.

**Response:** **Accepted, and delivered. The referee found a real gap, and closing it turned out to be more interesting than expected.**

The package carried generation scripts in `data-raw/` for `cnefe_index_2022` and for `tracts_variables_ref`, both public in the repository. The UF-level census tract Parquet assets served from GitHub Releases had none. They were built once, published, and the code that built them was never committed. The referee could not have known that from the manuscript, which is exactly their point.

**The generation script now exists and is verified.**

`data-raw/sc_assets_build.R` builds every asset from source. It was reconstructed from the published files rather than from notes, so we verified it against them rather than asserting it. Tract by tract, on Amapá:

| | published | rebuilt |
|---|---|---|
| rows | 1,492 | 1,492 |
| unique tract codes | 1,492 | 1,492 |
| geometries with identical area | — | **1,492 of 1,492 (100.00%)** |
| total area | 142,582.7 km² | 142,582.7 km² (+0.00%) |
| attribute variables reproducing exactly | — | **24 of 24** |

The per-variable check is committed as `data-raw/sc_assets_build_verification.csv`.

**Reconstructing it exposed two things the written record got wrong.**

**The variable codes point somewhere other than where they appear to**, since the codes recorded in `tracts_variables_ref` (`V00005`, `V01007`, `V06001`) could not be found in the IBGE tract aggregates published on the FTP server, and `V06001` and `V06004` appear in no 2022 file at all. That briefly suggested the assets might be mixing census editions, but they are not. The codes refer to **censobr** (Pereira and Barbosa, 2026), which repackages the same aggregates and prefixes each variable with its source table, so `V00005` arrives as `domicilio01_V00005`, except in `ResponsavelRenda` where the codes are bare. The `table_ibge` column of our own reference table corresponds to censobr datasets rather than IBGE files, which was documented nowhere.

**A correctness hazard was sitting in the build,** as geobr returns some tracts as several rows, one per disjoint part, carrying identical attributes. This is not rare: 7 such rows for Amapá, 1,026 for Pará, 1,921 for Amazonas. Left as they are, each row enters the spatial join separately and counts that tract's CNEFE points two or three times. The published assets dissolve them, which is how we recovered the intended behaviour: for tract `160010505000008` the published geometry measures 490.313 km², exactly the union of its two parts at 91.273 and 399.041 km². The reconstructed script now dissolves them explicitly and says why.

Neither of these could have been recovered from the package as it stood. That is the substance of the referee's concern, and we would not have found either without acting on it.

**Checksums.**

`data-raw/sc_assets_checksums.csv` records the SHA-256 and size of every published asset, 27 files and about 1.22 GB per release, against the release tag they are served under. A user can verify that the file they received is the file we shipped. We also recorded, in the code that resolves release tags, the constraint this creates: a published edition's tag must never be renamed, because the checksums are computed against it.

**The assets are now served from a release the script builds.**

Once the script was verified, we rebuilt all 27 states with it and published the result as a new release, `sc-assets-v3`, which the package now uses. Compared tract by tract with the original release (`sc-assets-v2`), it has the same 468,097 tracts in all 27 states, and all 3,144,868 value comparisons are identical, as recorded state by state in `data-raw/sc_assets_regen_verification.csv`. The old release stays published, so earlier versions of the package keep working, and the checksums of both releases are recorded. So the files users download are no longer only reproducible in principle, they are the output of the committed script.

**On the `targets` workflow.**

We take the referee's own fallback, "or at least documenting the existing asset-generation pipeline more explicitly". Rebuilding asset generation as a reproducible `targets` pipeline modelled on geobr is the right long-term design and we intend to move that way. It is infrastructure work we cannot deliver responsibly inside a revision window, and delivering it badly would be worse than the honest record we now have. What the referee asks for in substance is auditability, and a verified generation script plus published checksums delivers that.

**The provenance statement in the manuscript.**

Section 3 now ends with a "Data provenance" subsection. It names the scripts that build the index and the census tract assets, says where the geometries and attributes come from (geobr and censobr, now cited), explains the dissolving of multipart tracts, and gives the release tag, the verification result and where the checksums are. Table 3 now says that its variable codes are the ones used by censobr, rather than calling them IBGE codes, and `?tracts_variables_ref` says the same.

### R1.10: Memory Inefficiency in Pure-R Fallbacks

> **Memory Inefficiency in Pure-R Fallbacks:** In the pure R backends (e.g., within `.cnefe_counts_user_poly_r` and `.cnefe_counts_h3`), the code calls `as.data.frame(tab)` directly on the imported Arrow table before applying `dplyr::filter()` and `dplyr::select()`. For massive datasets like São Paulo (5.7 million records), materialising the entire dataset in memory before filtering completely negates the memory advantages of reading with Arrow. The authors should apply the `dplyr` verbs directly to the Arrow Table and call `dplyr::collect()` as the final step before converting to `sf`.

**Response:** **Accepted and implemented, with one qualification to the diagnosis.**

The four pure-R backends now apply `transmute()` and `filter()` to the Arrow table and call `collect()` last, exactly as the referee prescribes.

We measured before and after, because the size of the effect matters for how we describe it:

| | rows | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lauro de Freitas-BA | 111k | 49.6 MB | 47.1 MB | |
| Fortaleza-CE | 1.19M | 108.4 MB | 68.3 MB | **-37%** |

The saving scales with row count and costs roughly 0.2s, the usual trade of time for memory. On a small municipality it is not measurable, which is expected.

Importantly, the qualification concerns the mechanism rather than the fix. The referee writes that materialising first "completely negates the memory advantages of reading with Arrow". That is only partly so. `read_cnefe()` returns an in-memory `arrow::Table`, so the Arrow data is already resident before any backend touches it. What `as.data.frame()` added was a **second** full copy, as an R data frame of all 34 columns, of which three were then kept. That second copy is what the change removes, and it is the larger of the two.

Getting the full effect the referee has in mind would require `read_cnefe()` to return a lazy Arrow dataset rather than a materialised table. We considered that under R1.11 and declined it there, for reasons that have nothing to do with this item.

Two other `as.data.frame()` calls remain and are deliberate. `read_cnefe(output = "sf")` and `cnefe_export()` are both asked for every column, so there is nothing to push down. Both now carry a comment saying so, since the pattern otherwise looks like the one just fixed.

The regression test guards the translation rather than the output and Arrow falls back to R when it cannot translate an expression, which would silently restore the old memory profile while leaving every result identical. Therefore, a test that only compared values would never notice.

### R1.11: Architecture Consistency & Efficiency in `read_cnefe()`

> **Architecture Consistency & Efficiency in `read_cnefe()`:** The current implementation of `read_cnefe()` extracts the ZIP file to a temporary directory using `utils::unzip()` before reading it with `arrow::read_delim_arrow()`. This "unpack-every-time" approach is somewhat wasteful in terms of disk I/O and CPU. While using DuckDB's `zipfs` for zero-extraction streaming is a valid alternative, reading directly from ZIP archives can be computationally expensive for repeated queries. Empirical benchmarks using the Salvador dataset (1.3M rows) show that reading from standard ZIP archives via `zipfs` is significantly slower than native alternatives. Specifically, Gzip was **2.2x faster** than ZIP, and raw CSV was **4.7x faster**. The authors might consider re-compressing the cached data into `.gz` (Gzip) format. DuckDB supports Gzip decompression natively in its core, which avoids the protocol overhead of the community `zipfs` extension. Beyond performance, the authors might also consider the potential stability risks of relying on community-maintained DuckDB extensions in an R package. Some community extensions (e.g., `onager`) are known to encounter issues on macOS due to lack of code-signing and GateKeeper whitelisting. This can cause significant loading delays (4-5 seconds) as the OS re-verifies the extension on every load. While it is unclear if `zipfs` suffers from this specific issue, minimising the surface area of external community dependencies is generally considered a safer practice for production-grade R packages when native alternatives (like Gzip or Parquet) are available. Another resilient option would be to provide a conversion/reorganisation function that allows users to move data from the transient cache to a persistent, optimised structure (like raw CSV or Parquet) on a disk of their choice (see the `spanishoddata` package for an example of this design). Moving toward a lazy DuckDB/DuckSpatial relation (potentially via `duckspatial_df`) instead of a materialised `arrow::Table` would complete this transition to a modern, memory-efficient architecture. I have included three small supplementary scripts: `benchmark_gz_vs_zip.R`, which benchmarks ZIP/`zipfs` reads against native Gzip and raw CSV on the Salvador data; and `suggested_duckdb_impl.R` and `test_duckdb_zipfs.R`, which demonstrate the basic DuckDB/`zipfs` approach. They are not proposed as drop-in production code, but they may help clarify the implementation pattern and provide a starting point for more formal package tests or benchmarks.

**Response:** **Three of the referee's four suggestions are implemented. We decline the fourth, and the reason is that it conflicts with what the referees themselves asked for elsewhere.**

This was the largest single item in either report, and we treated it as four separate proposals.

**Re-compressing the cache to Gzip: implemented, after reproducing the measurement.**

We did not take the referee's figures on trust, and we are glad we did not, because the decision turned on a term their benchmark does not include: the one-time cost of converting the published ZIP into whatever we cache instead.

Our run, using their `benchmark_gz_vs_zip.R` as the starting point, with DuckDB reading the full file, median of three repetitions:

| | zip | gz | csv | conversion | break-even |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lauro de Freitas-BA | 1.25s | 1.21s | 0.65s | 0.52s | 15.3 reads |
| Fortaleza-CE | 5.45s | 2.38s | 1.12s | 14.32s | 4.7 reads |

Their numbers reproduce closely: 2.29x for gzip against their reported 2.2x, and 4.86x for raw CSV against their 4.7x.

Two findings settled it. **Gzip costs nothing on disk**, 27.6 MB against the ZIP's 27.6 MB, whereas raw CSV needs 184.1 MB, 6.7 times more, which is why we did not adopt the fastest option. And **the conversion has to be earned back**, in roughly five reads on a mid-size municipality.

The cache now holds a gzipped CSV. The conversion runs once, on first download, streamed in chunks so peak memory does not scale with the file, and writes through a temporary name so an interrupted run cannot leave something that later passes for a valid cache entry.

**Reducing reliance on community extensions: implemented.**

The referee's aside about community DuckDB extensions, including macOS code-signing delays of 4 to 5 seconds per load, weighed more with us than the throughput figures. That cost is paid per connection, and the package opens a connection in every function.

Because DuckDB decompresses gzip natively, **`zipfs` is no longer loaded on any connection**. It is ensured on demand, only when the file at hand is actually a ZIP, which now happens solely for a cache written by an earlier version or a file the user supplies directly. We could not measure the macOS delay from our platform, so we report the referee's figure as theirs rather than confirming it.

**A conversion function to a persistent store: implemented.**

New `cnefe_export(code_muni, path, format)` writes a municipality where the user wants it, as Parquet (the default), CSV or gzipped CSV. `read_cnefe()` gains a `file` argument that reads any of those, and also the raw ZIP as IBGE publishes it, skipping retrieval entirely.

This follows `spanishoddata`, which the referee cites. It also answers Referee 2's R2.7, where the same separation is asked for from the opposite direction, namely whether the package could ingest a locally obtained file if access policy changed. Both paths share the same output code, so they return the same object for the same data.

**A lazy DuckDB relation: declined, and we ask the referee to weigh the reason.**

This is the one suggestion we did not take. A lazy relation, `tbl(con, ...)` in the referee's `suggested_duckdb_impl.R`, is valid only while its connection is alive. Returning one from `read_cnefe()` requires the connection to outlive the call, with ownership transferred to the returned object and released by a finalizer or an explicit close.

That is precisely the pattern **both referees asked us to remove**. Referee 1's R1.12 and Referee 2's R2.C3 identify connections whose cleanup was not deterministic, and R1.12 recommends `withr::defer()` by name. We adopted it and every connection now registers a guarded cleanup on its caller's frame immediately after `dbConnect()` returns. Adopting the lazy relation would reintroduce, deliberately, the class of leak we were asked to eliminate.

It is also a breaking change to the return type. `read_cnefe()` currently returns an `arrow::Table` or an `sf` object, and a lazy relation is a third type with different semantics, which four internal code paths and two published articles assume.

We think the memory-efficiency goal behind the suggestion is better served by the parts we did adopt: the export function moves users to Parquet, which is columnar and read lazily, and the pure-R backends now push their filters down to Arrow before collecting, addressed under R1.10.

In the manuscript, Section 3 describes the gzipped cache and the export path, Section 4.5 shows `cnefe_export()` and `read_cnefe(file = ...)` in use, and Section 6 explains to readers why `read_cnefe()` returns a materialised object and how to query a very large municipality lazily from an exported Parquet file.

### R1.12: Resource Cleanup and Connection Leaks

> **Resource Cleanup and Connection Leaks:** In several DuckDB backend functions (e.g., `.cnefe_counts_h3`, `compute_lumi`, `tracts_to_h3`), the connection `con` is initialized to `NULL`, followed by a large `utils::capture.output` block that performs the `DBI::dbConnect` and subsequent queries. The `on.exit(DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE))` call is only registered *after* this block completes. If an error occurs inside the block—such as an extension loading failure, a memory-intensive SQL error, or a manual user interruption—the function exits before the cleanup is registered, leaving "zombie" DuckDB processes and file handles active. The authors should move the `on.exit()` registration to immediately follow the `dbConnect()` call (even if it's inside the `capture.output` block) to ensure connections are always closed. Alternatively, the authors could adopt the `withr::defer()` pattern for cleaner resource management. Additionally, wrapping the cleanup in a safety check like `if (!is.null(con) && DBI::dbIsValid(con))` is a defensive best practice to prevent secondary errors during cleanup if the connection failed to initialize.

**Response:** **Accepted in full, including the referee's suggested pattern.**

The referee's reading of the failure mode is exact. `on.exit()` was registered only after the whole `capture.output` block had run, so an extension install failure, a SQL error or a user interrupt exited before any cleanup was in place.

We audited every connection site rather than only the ones named. Of the six, four registered `on.exit()` between 20 and 56 lines after `dbConnect()`, outside the block, one registered none at all and disconnected manually at the end of the function, and one was acceptable.

All six now route through a single internal helper that opens the connection and registers cleanup on the caller's frame immediately, before any extension load can fail. We took the referee's alternative suggestion and used `withr::defer()`, which made the helper considerably cleaner than manipulating `on.exit()` across frames, and we added `withr` to Imports for it. The handler is guarded with `!is.null(con) && DBI::dbIsValid(con)`, the defensive check the referee recommends.

We verified both paths explicitly and the connection is closed when the caller returns normally, and when the caller aborts mid-block.

### R1.13: Test Coverage & Quality

> **Test Coverage & Quality:** While the package includes a `testthat` suite with good use of mocks for offline testing of `read_cnefe()`, the overall package coverage is relatively low at ~25%. Specifically, critical spatial transformation functions such as `tracts_to_h3()` and `tracts_to_polygon()` currently have 0% and ~10% coverage, respectively. Given the complexity of the geospatial logic and the dual-backend architecture, I strongly encourage the authors to expand the test suite to ensure the reliability of these core components.

**Response:** **Accepted.**

We added tests, and coverage rose for the package as a whole and for `tracts_to_polygon()` in particular. The 0% for `tracts_to_h3()` has a specific cause, explained below.

Coverage depends on how it's measured. Under CRAN's defaults, tests marked with `skip_on_cran()` don't run, and that is the measurement behind the referee's figures. With `NOT_CRAN=true`, which is how the tests run during development and in continuous integration on GitHub, every test runs. Before and after this revision:

| | CRAN defaults | Full run (`NOT_CRAN=true`) |
|---|---|---|
| Whole package | 38.3% → **46.3%** | 58.3% → **69.2%** |
| `R/tracts_to_polygon.R` | 10.8% → 10.8% | 10.8% → **83.3%** |
| `R/tracts_to_h3.R` | 0.0% → 0.0% | 90.0% → 90.0% |
| `R/utils-internal.R` | 34.5% → **51.9%** | 58.2% → 60.4% |

`tracts_to_polygon()` used to have tests for input validation only. It now has tests that check its output, built so the expected values are exact: a polygon covering a tract receives exactly the tract's allocated total, a tract split between two polygons is divided correctly, the caller's columns and CRS are kept, `crs_output` works, and the two-stage diagnostics are reported. They're described in more detail under R2.C8.

`tracts_to_h3()` already had an end-to-end test of its output, which covers 90% of the file. The referee's 0% is what CRAN's defaults produce, because that test calls `skip_on_cran()`. Checking this for the present response, we found that the test was also being skipped in our own continuous integration, on all four machines, because it still required the DuckDB `zipfs` extension, which the package stopped needing when the cache became a gzipped CSV (R1.11). We removed that requirement, and the test, along with one other that had the same problem, now runs on every machine.

The logic of both functions now also runs on CRAN. The deduplication Referee 2 asked for in R2.C1 moved the allocation rules and the diagnostics out of `tracts_to_h3()` and `tracts_to_polygon()` into shared internal helpers (`.build_alloc_sql()`, `.build_interp_diagnostics()` and `.report_interp_diagnostics()`). These helpers need only core DuckDB, with no extension, so we test them directly and without `skip_on_cran()`. That is where the rise in `R/utils-internal.R` under CRAN's defaults comes from, and it means the calculations themselves are now tested on CRAN, even though the two files still show the figures above.

We kept `skip_on_cran()` on the end-to-end tests because of a crash. It was added in version 0.2.1 after the DuckDB spatial extension caused a segfault on CRAN's `r-devel-linux-x86_64-fedora-clang` check machine, an incompatibility between the clang-built DuckDB binary and the GCC-built extension (duckdb/duckdb-r#1107). Removing it would risk the package failing on CRAN again, so we'd rather report the 0% plainly than raise it by dropping a skip that guards against a segfault.
